title: classify the bonding in a solid from a set of property data, resisting a single misleading cue (low melting temperature)
stem: Substance Q is a silvery solid that can be cut with a knife. It conducts electricity as a solid, can be hammered into thin sheets without breaking, and melts at 98°C. A student reasons that the low melting temperature shows that Q consists of separate molecules held together by weak forces. Which statement is best supported by all of the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Q is a molecular solid, because a low melting temperature always indicates weak attractions between separate molecules.
choices.rationale: Molecular solids do not conduct electricity as solids and are not malleable, so these data contradict a molecular model even though the melting temperature is low.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Q is an ionic solid, because its metal atoms have transferred electrons to nonmetal atoms in a lattice.
choices.rationale: Ionic solids are brittle and do not conduct as solids, because their ions are fixed in the lattice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Q is a metallic solid; conduction as a solid and malleability require delocalized electrons shared among metal cations, and the low melting temperature only shows that these attractions are comparatively weak.
choices.rationale: Correct: conduction in the solid state plus malleability point to a sea of delocalized electrons around metal cations, so the bonding is metallic. A low melting temperature is consistent with metallic bonding that is weak, such as in sodium, 98°C.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Q is a network covalent solid, because covalent bonds between neighboring atoms allow it to conduct as a solid.
choices.rationale: Network covalent solids are very hard with very high melting temperatures, and their electrons are localized in bonds, so they are not malleable.

title: classify the bonding in a solid from a set of property data, resisting a single misleading cue (low melting temperature) (variant 1)
stem: Substance R is a gray solid that conducts electricity both as a solid and as a liquid. It can be pressed into a new shape without shattering, and it melts at 30°C, just above room temperature. A student argues that because R melts so easily it must be a molecular compound. Which statement is best supported by all of the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: R is a molecular solid, because substances with melting temperatures near room temperature are always made of small molecules.
choices.rationale: Molecular solids have no mobile charge carriers and cannot conduct as solids, so the conductivity rules out a molecular model despite the low melting temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: R is an ionic solid, because it conducts electricity when it is a liquid.
choices.rationale: Ionic solids conduct only when molten or dissolved, not as solids, and they shatter when struck instead of changing shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: R is a metallic solid; its delocalized valence electrons explain conduction and shape change, and the low melting temperature simply means the attraction between cations and electrons is relatively weak.
choices.rationale: Correct: conduction as a solid and malleability require mobile delocalized electrons, which identifies metallic bonding; gallium is a real example, melting at about 30°C.

choices.label: D
choices.text: R is a network covalent solid, because covalent bonds hold the atoms together in a continuous array that can be reshaped.
choices.rationale: Network covalent solids have very high melting temperatures, and covalent networks are rigid and would fracture rather than be pressed into shape.

title: classify the bonding in a solid from a set of property data, resisting a single misleading cue (low melting temperature) (variant 2)
stem: Substance S is a colorless crystal that does not conduct electricity as a solid or when molten, is extremely hard, does not dissolve in water, and melts above 1700°C. A student concludes that the high melting temperature shows S is ionic. Which statement is best supported by all of the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: S is an ionic solid, because only ionic attractions are strong enough to give a melting temperature above 1700°C.
choices.rationale: An ionic compound would conduct once it is molten because its ions would be free to move, and S does not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: S is a metallic solid, because very hard solids with high melting temperatures contain a sea of delocalized electrons.
choices.rationale: A metallic solid would conduct electricity as a solid, which S does not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: S is a molecular solid, because it is a nonconductor and nonconductors are always made of discrete molecules.
choices.rationale: Molecular solids have weak forces between molecules and melt at low temperatures, so they cannot be extremely hard with a melting temperature above 1700°C.

choices.label: D
choices.text: S is a network covalent solid; each atom is covalently bonded to its neighbors in a continuous three-dimensional array, so there are no mobile ions or electrons and melting requires breaking many covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: Correct: a nonconductor in both solid and molten states has no mobile ions, which rules out ionic bonding; extreme hardness and a very high melting temperature indicate a covalent network, as in quartz or diamond.

title: classify the bonding in a solid from a set of property data, resisting a single misleading cue (low melting temperature) (variant 3)
stem: Substance T is a white, brittle solid that does not conduct electricity as a solid but conducts well when molten at 650°C. A student concludes that T is a metal because it conducts when molten. Which statement is best supported by all of the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: T is a metallic solid, because any substance that conducts electricity when molten must contain delocalized electrons.
choices.rationale: A metal would conduct as a solid, and T does not, so molten conductivity alone cannot distinguish metallic from ionic bonding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: T is a network covalent solid, because it is brittle and the melting temperature is high.
choices.rationale: Network covalent solids do not conduct when molten because they have no mobile ions or electrons, whereas T does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: T is a molecular solid, because it is a nonconductor in the solid state.
choices.rationale: Molecular solids do not conduct when molten either, because neutral molecules carry no charge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: T is an ionic solid; its ions are fixed in a lattice in the solid, so it does not conduct, and they become mobile charge carriers when T melts.
choices.rationale: Correct: nonconductor as a solid, brittle, and conducting only when molten is the pattern for an ionic solid; the charge carriers when molten are ions, not electrons.

title: use electronegativity values to determine the direction of bond polarity, including cases where hydrogen is the more ele
stem: Pauling electronegativities: H 2.20, C 2.55, Si 1.90. A student states that in any bond to hydrogen, the hydrogen atom carries the partial positive charge. Which statement correctly gives the partial charge on the hydrogen atom in the C–H bonds of CH₄ and in the Si–H bonds of SiH₄?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ in CH₄ and δ− in SiH₄, because the shared electrons are drawn toward the more electronegative atom in each bond.
choices.rationale: Correct: in C–H the difference is 2.55 − 2.20 = 0.35 with C more electronegative, so H is δ+; in Si–H the difference is 2.20 − 1.90 = 0.30 with H more electronegative, so H is δ−.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ in both CH₄ and SiH₄, because hydrogen is always the less electronegative partner.
choices.rationale: Hydrogen is not always the less electronegative atom; silicon at 1.90 is less electronegative than hydrogen at 2.20, so the polarity reverses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen carries no partial charge in either molecule, because C, Si and H all form covalent bonds by sharing electrons.
choices.rationale: Sharing electrons does not make the sharing equal, and unequal electronegativities give polar covalent bonds with partial charges.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ− in CH₄ and δ+ in SiH₄, because the larger electronegativity difference makes it more negative.
choices.rationale: This reverses both directions, because carbon at 2.55 attracts the shared pair more than hydrogen and hydrogen attracts it more than silicon.

title: use electronegativity values to determine the direction of bond polarity, including cases where hydrogen is the more ele (variant 1)
stem: Pauling electronegativities: H 2.20, B 2.04, N 3.04. Which statement correctly gives the partial charge on the hydrogen atom in BH₃ and in NH₃?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ in both BH₃ and NH₃.
choices.rationale: It assumes that hydrogen is always the positive end, but boron is less electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pair shifts toward hydrogen in BH₃.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ− in BH₃ and δ+ in NH₃.
choices.rationale: Correct: in B–H, H (2.20) is more electronegative than B (2.04), so H is δ−; in N–H, N (3.04) is more electronegative than H (2.20), so H is δ+.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ in BH₃ and δ− in NH₃.
choices.rationale: This reverses the polarity of both bonds and ignores that nitrogen at 3.04 pulls the shared pair away from hydrogen at 2.20.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ− in both BH₃ and NH₃, because hydrogen has only one electron to share.
choices.rationale: The number of valence electrons an atom has does not set bond polarity, and nitrogen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen.

title: use electronegativity values to determine the direction of bond polarity, including cases where hydrogen is the more ele (variant 2)
stem: Pauling electronegativities: H 2.20, Na 0.93, Br 2.96. Which statement correctly describes the charge on the hydrogen atom in the compound NaH and in the molecule HBr?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ or positively charged in both NaH and HBr.
choices.rationale: This treats hydrogen as the positive end of every bond, but sodium at 0.93 is far less electronegative than hydrogen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen is negatively charged in NaH, and it carries a partial positive charge in HBr.
choices.rationale: Correct: in NaH the electronegativity difference is 2.20 − 0.93 = 1.27 with H more electronegative, so H is the negative end; in HBr, Br at 2.96 is more electronegative than H at 2.20, so H is δ+.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen is negatively charged in HBr and positively charged in NaH.
choices.rationale: This reverses both cases, because bromine at 2.96 attracts the shared pair more than hydrogen and hydrogen attracts the electrons more than sodium does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrogen is neutral in NaH and δ+ in HBr, because only HBr has a difference in electronegativity.
choices.rationale: NaH also has a large electronegativity difference, 1.27, so hydrogen is not neutral there.

title: use electronegativity values to determine the direction of bond polarity, including cases where hydrogen is the more ele (variant 3)
stem: Pauling electronegativities: H 2.20, Ge 2.01, O 3.44. Which statement correctly gives the partial charge on the hydrogen atoms in GeH₄ and in H₂O?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ in both GeH₄ and H₂O, because it is the smallest atom in each molecule.
choices.rationale: Atomic size does not decide polarity, which depends on electronegativity, and germanium at 2.01 is less electronegative than hydrogen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ+ in GeH₄ and δ− in H₂O.
choices.rationale: This reverses both bonds, since oxygen is the more electronegative atom in water and hydrogen is the more electronegative atom in GeH₄.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ− in GeH₄ and δ+ in H₂O.
choices.rationale: Correct: in Ge–H, H (2.20) exceeds Ge (2.01) so H is δ−; in O–H, O (3.44) exceeds H (2.20) so H is δ+.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrogen is δ− in both GeH₄ and H₂O, because it is bonded to a central atom in each.
choices.rationale: Being bonded to a central atom does not make hydrogen negative, and in water oxygen draws the electrons away from hydrogen.

title: read bond length (position of the minimum) and bond energy (depth of the minimum) from potential-energy data, without as
stem:
Potential energy (PE) is defined as 0 kJ/mol for fully separated atoms. A student records PE for two hypothetical diatomic molecules, X₂ and Y₂, at several internuclear distances.
Distance (pm): 90, 110, 130, 150, 170
PE of X₂ (kJ/mol): +50, −300, −180, −90, −30
PE of Y₂ (kJ/mol): +900, −200, −430, −520, −400
Which statement correctly compares the two molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Y₂ has the longer bond, and Y₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: Correct: the minimum for X₂ is −300 kJ/mol at 110 pm and for Y₂ is −520 kJ/mol at 150 pm. Bond length is the distance at the minimum (150 pm > 110 pm, so Y₂ is longer) and bond energy is the depth of the minimum (520 > 300 kJ/mol, so Y₂ is stronger).

choices.label: B
choices.text: X₂ has the longer bond, and X₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It reads both quantities for the wrong molecule; the lowest PE and the larger distance both belong to Y₂.

choices.label: C
choices.text: X₂ has the longer bond, and Y₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It reverses the bond lengths, because the PE minimum of X₂ occurs at the shorter distance, 110 pm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Y₂ has the longer bond, and X₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It applies the rule that the longer bond must be the weaker one, but bond energy is the depth of the well, and Y₂ has the deeper well at the longer distance.

title: read bond length (position of the minimum) and bond energy (depth of the minimum) from potential-energy data, without as (variant 1)
stem:
PE is 0 kJ/mol for separated atoms. A student records PE for two hypothetical diatomic molecules, P₂ and Q₂.
Distance (pm): 90, 105, 120, 135, 150
PE of P₂ (kJ/mol): +350, −40, −250, −390, −310
PE of Q₂ (kJ/mol): −300, −520, −420, −250, −140
Which statement correctly compares the two molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P₂ has the shorter bond, and P₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It assigns both properties to P₂, but P₂ has the minimum at the larger distance and the shallower well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P₂ has the shorter bond, and Q₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It correctly sees that Q₂ is deeper but reads the distance of P₂ as the shorter one, when its minimum is at 135 pm and not 105 pm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Q₂ has the shorter bond, and Q₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: Correct: P₂ has its minimum of −390 kJ/mol at 135 pm and Q₂ has its minimum of −520 kJ/mol at 105 pm, so Q₂ has both the shorter bond and the larger bond energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Q₂ has the shorter bond, and P₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It correctly places Q₂ at the shorter distance but then claims P₂ is stronger, when the well of P₂ is only 390 kJ/mol deep and the well of Q₂ is 520 kJ/mol deep.

title: read bond length (position of the minimum) and bond energy (depth of the minimum) from potential-energy data, without as (variant 2)
stem:
PE is 0 kJ/mol for separated atoms. A student records PE for two hypothetical diatomic molecules, U₂ and V₂.
Distance (pm): 80, 100, 120, 140, 160
PE of U₂ (kJ/mol): +120, −210, −150, −80, −40
PE of V₂ (kJ/mol): +900, +120, −300, −460, −380
Which statement correctly compares the two molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: U₂ has the longer bond, and V₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It reverses the lengths, but the minimum of U₂ is at 100 pm, which is shorter than the 140 pm of V₂.

choices.label: B
choices.text: U₂ has the longer bond, and U₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It assigns both properties to U₂, which has the shorter bond and the shallower well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: V₂ has the longer bond, and U₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It uses the rule that a longer bond is a weaker bond, but bond energy is the depth of the well, which is larger for V₂ at 460 kJ/mol than for U₂ at 210 kJ/mol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: V₂ has the longer bond, and V₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: Correct: U₂ has its minimum of −210 kJ/mol at 100 pm and V₂ has its minimum of −460 kJ/mol at 140 pm, so V₂ is both longer and stronger.

title: read bond length (position of the minimum) and bond energy (depth of the minimum) from potential-energy data, without as (variant 3)
stem:
PE is 0 kJ/mol for separated atoms. A student records PE for two hypothetical diatomic molecules, K₂ and L₂.
Distance (pm): 100, 120, 140, 160, 180
PE of K₂ (kJ/mol): +150, −120, −250, −290, −230
PE of L₂ (kJ/mol): +500, −200, −350, −270, −190
Which statement correctly compares the two molecules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: L₂ has the shorter bond, and L₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: Correct: K₂ has its minimum of −290 kJ/mol at 160 pm and L₂ has its minimum of −350 kJ/mol at 140 pm, so L₂ has the shorter bond and the larger bond energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: K₂ has the shorter bond, and L₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It reads the bond length of K₂ as the shorter one, but its minimum is at 160 pm and not at 140 pm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: K₂ has the shorter bond, and K₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It assigns both properties to K₂, which has the longer bond and the shallower well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: L₂ has the shorter bond, and K₂ has the greater bond energy.
choices.rationale: It places L₂ at the shorter distance correctly but says K₂ is stronger, even though the well of L₂ is deeper at 350 kJ/mol against 290 kJ/mol.

title: use a potential-energy curve to predict the direction of the net force and the motion of two atoms released from rest at
stem: For two hydrogen atoms, PE is 0 kJ/mol when they are far apart. The PE is −436 kJ/mol at the equilibrium distance of 74 pm, −300 kJ/mol at 60 pm, and −300 kJ/mol at 100 pm. Two hydrogen atoms are released from rest when their nuclei are 60 pm apart. Which description is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The net force is repulsive, because electron and nucleus repulsions outweigh attractions inside 74 pm; the atoms move apart, and PE decreases as kinetic energy increases until 74 pm.
choices.rationale: Correct: at 60 pm the PE is higher than the minimum, and PE decreases as the distance increases toward 74 pm, so the net force pushes the atoms apart. The total energy of −300 kJ/mol is below zero, so the atoms remain bound.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The atoms move closer together, because their PE is negative and negative PE means the net force is attractive.
choices.rationale: The sign of the PE does not give the direction of the force, which depends on whether PE falls or rises as the distance changes, and PE falls as the atoms move apart from 60 pm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The atoms stay at 60 pm, because any distance with negative PE is stable.
choices.rationale: Only the minimum at 74 pm is an equilibrium distance, and at 60 pm the PE is above the minimum so a net force acts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The atoms separate completely, because repulsion at short distances always exceeds the energy that holds the atoms together.
choices.rationale: The total energy is −300 kJ/mol, which is below zero, so the atoms cannot escape to infinite separation without gaining energy.

title: use a potential-energy curve to predict the direction of the net force and the motion of two atoms released from rest at (variant 1)
stem: For two nitrogen atoms in N₂, PE is 0 kJ/mol when the atoms are far apart, −945 kJ/mol at the equilibrium distance of 110 pm, and −500 kJ/mol at 150 pm. Two nitrogen atoms are released from rest when their nuclei are 150 pm apart. Which description is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The net force is repulsive, because PE is negative and the atoms are farther apart than at equilibrium.
choices.rationale: At distances greater than the equilibrium distance, attractions between nuclei and electrons outweigh repulsions, so the net force is attractive and not repulsive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The net force is attractive; the atoms move closer together, PE decreases, and kinetic energy increases until the distance is 110 pm.
choices.rationale: Correct: at 150 pm, PE (−500) is above the minimum (−945 at 110 pm), and PE falls as the distance decreases toward 110 pm, so the net force is attractive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The atoms remain at 150 pm, because the PE there is negative.
choices.rationale: A negative PE alone does not make a distance an equilibrium, and the atoms feel a net force because PE changes with distance at 150 pm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The atoms drift apart until they are free atoms, because the PE at 150 pm is higher than at 110 pm.
choices.rationale: The total energy of −500 kJ/mol is below zero, so the atoms are bound and cannot separate completely without added energy.

title: use a potential-energy curve to predict the direction of the net force and the motion of two atoms released from rest at (variant 2)
stem: For two chlorine atoms in Cl₂, PE is 0 kJ/mol when the atoms are far apart, −243 kJ/mol at the equilibrium distance of 199 pm, and −120 kJ/mol at 170 pm. Two chlorine atoms are released from rest when their nuclei are 170 pm apart. Which description is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The atoms move closer together, because PE is negative and the atoms were released from rest.
choices.rationale: Moving closer from 170 pm would raise PE and need energy input, so a released pair moves toward the lower PE at 199 pm, which is farther apart.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The atoms do not move, because the PE at 170 pm is negative and so the atoms are stable.
choices.rationale: Only the equilibrium distance has zero net force, and at 170 pm the atoms feel a net repulsion even though PE is negative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The atoms fly apart and separate completely, because a distance shorter than 199 pm always means the atoms repel enough to break the bond.
choices.rationale: The total energy of −120 kJ/mol is below zero, so the atoms oscillate about 199 pm without breaking apart.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The net force is repulsive; the atoms move apart, passing through 199 pm with their maximum kinetic energy.
choices.rationale: Correct: at 170 pm the PE (−120) is higher than the minimum (−243 at 199 pm), so PE falls as the atoms separate and the net force is repulsive; the kinetic energy is greatest where PE is lowest, at 199 pm.

title: use a potential-energy curve to predict the direction of the net force and the motion of two atoms released from rest at (variant 3)
stem: For the H–Br bond, PE is 0 kJ/mol when the atoms are far apart, −366 kJ/mol at the equilibrium distance of 141 pm, and −100 kJ/mol at 220 pm. A hydrogen atom and a bromine atom are released from rest when their nuclei are 220 pm apart. Which description is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The net force is repulsive, because the atoms are farther apart than their equilibrium distance.
choices.rationale: Beyond the equilibrium distance, the attraction between nuclei and electrons outweighs the repulsions, so the force is attractive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The atoms stay at 220 pm, because they are neutral atoms and exert no net force.
choices.rationale: Neutral atoms still attract through electron and nucleus interactions at these distances, and the PE value of −100 kJ/mol shows the interaction is not zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The net force is attractive; the atoms move closer together as PE decreases and kinetic energy increases toward 141 pm.
choices.rationale: Correct: the PE at 220 pm (−100) is above the minimum, and PE falls as the atoms approach 141 pm, so the force is attractive and the atoms speed up as they approach.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The atoms move apart to infinite separation, because the PE at 220 pm is higher than the PE at 141 pm.
choices.rationale: A system with negative total energy cannot separate to infinity, and the lower PE at 141 pm means the atoms move toward it and not away.

title: apply Coulomb's law quantitatively, using ion charges and the sum of ionic radii, to compare the strength of ionic attra
stem: Approximate ionic radii (pm): Mg²⁺ 72, O²⁻ 140, Na⁺ 102, F⁻ 133. Treat the distance between neighboring ions as the sum of the ionic radii. The magnitude of the electrostatic potential energy of a cation-anion pair is proportional to (charge of cation × charge of anion) ÷ distance. About how many times larger is this magnitude for a neighboring Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ pair in MgO than for a neighboring Na⁺ and F⁻ pair in NaF?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 4.4 times larger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 2.0 times, because the sum of the charges of the ions in MgO is twice the sum in NaF.
choices.rationale: Potential energy depends on the product of the charges and not on their sum, and the distance also differs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 4.9 times larger.
choices.rationale: This value is the ratio of the forces, 4 × (235/212)², because force varies as 1/d², whereas the potential energy varies as 1/d.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 4.0 times, because the charge product is 4 times larger and the distances are almost identical.
choices.rationale: It ignores the smaller distance in MgO, 212 pm against 235 pm, which raises the ratio above the charge-product ratio of 4.

title: apply Coulomb's law quantitatively, using ion charges and the sum of ionic radii, to compare the strength of ionic attra (variant 1)
stem: Approximate ionic radii (pm): Ca²⁺ 100, O²⁻ 140, Rb⁺ 152, Br⁻ 196. Treat the distance between neighboring ions as the sum of the ionic radii. The magnitude of the electrostatic potential energy of a cation-anion pair is proportional to (charge of cation × charge of anion) ÷ distance. About how many times larger is this magnitude for a neighboring Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ pair in CaO than for a neighboring Rb⁺ and Br⁻ pair in RbBr?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 8.4 times larger.
choices.rationale: This is the force ratio, 4 × (348/240)², which uses an inverse-square dependence, whereas potential energy depends on 1/d.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 4.0 times, because only the charge product matters and the ions are about the same size.
choices.rationale: It ignores that the RbBr ions are much larger, so the distance in RbBr is 348 pm against 240 pm in CaO.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 5.8 times larger.
choices.rationale: Correct: CaO distance = 100 + 140 = 240 pm, so 4/240 = 0.01667. RbBr distance = 152 + 196 = 348 pm, so 1/348 = 0.002874. Ratio = 5.80.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 2.0 times, because the cation and anion charges in CaO add to 4 and those in RbBr add to 2.
choices.rationale: The energy depends on the product of the charges, 2 × 2 against 1 × 1, and not on their sum, and the distances differ too.

title: apply Coulomb's law quantitatively, using ion charges and the sum of ionic radii, to compare the strength of ionic attra (variant 2)
stem: Approximate ionic radii (pm): Al³⁺ 54, O²⁻ 140, K⁺ 138, Br⁻ 196. Treat the distance between neighboring ions as the sum of the ionic radii. The magnitude of the electrostatic potential energy of a cation-anion pair is proportional to (charge of cation × charge of anion) ÷ distance. About how many times larger is this magnitude for a neighboring Al³⁺ and O²⁻ pair in Al₂O₃ than for a neighboring K⁺ and Br⁻ pair in KBr?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 6.0 times, because the charge product is 6 times larger.
choices.rationale: It leaves out the distance, but the ions in Al₂O₃ are much closer, 194 pm against 334 pm, which raises the ratio well above 6.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 17.8 times larger.
choices.rationale: This is the force ratio, 6 × (334/194)², since force depends on 1/d² while potential energy depends on 1/d.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 2.5 times, because the charges in Al₂O₃ add to 5 and those in KBr add to 2.
choices.rationale: Energy depends on the product of the charges, 3 × 2 against 1 × 1, and not on their sum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 10.3 times larger.
choices.rationale: Correct: Al₂O₃ distance = 54 + 140 = 194 pm, so 6/194 = 0.03093. KBr distance = 138 + 196 = 334 pm, so 1/334 = 0.002994. Ratio = 10.33.

title: apply Coulomb's law quantitatively, using ion charges and the sum of ionic radii, to compare the strength of ionic attra (variant 3)
stem: Approximate ionic radii (pm): Ba²⁺ 135, O²⁻ 140, Cs⁺ 167, I⁻ 220. Treat the distance between neighboring ions as the sum of the ionic radii. The magnitude of the electrostatic potential energy of a cation-anion pair is proportional to (charge of cation × charge of anion) ÷ distance. About how many times larger is this magnitude for a neighboring Ba²⁺ and O²⁻ pair in BaO than for a neighboring Cs⁺ and I⁻ pair in CsI?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 7.9 times larger.
choices.rationale: This is the force ratio, 4 × (387/275)², which treats the force law as the energy law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5.6 times larger.
choices.rationale: Correct: BaO distance = 135 + 140 = 275 pm, so 4/275 = 0.01455. CsI distance = 167 + 220 = 387 pm, so 1/387 = 0.002584. Ratio = 5.63.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 2.0 times, because the charges in BaO add to 4 and those in CsI add to 2.
choices.rationale: Potential energy depends on the product of the charges, 4 against 1, and not on their sum, and the distance also differs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 4.0 times, because the ion sizes do not change the result.
choices.rationale: It ignores the distance, but the ions in CsI are far apart at 387 pm against 275 pm in BaO, so the ratio exceeds 4.

title: explain electrical conductivity data for an ionic compound in terms of mobile charged particles in the lattice, liquid a
stem:
A student tests the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride in three forms and records the results.
Solid NaCl crystals: no current
Molten NaCl at 801°C: large current
NaCl dissolved in water: large current
Which explanation is consistent with all three results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the solid, the ions are present but cannot carry charge; when NaCl melts, its ions are converted to Na and Cl atoms that share delocalized electrons.
choices.rationale: Ions do not convert to atoms with delocalized electrons on melting, since the liquid still consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, and this describes metallic bonding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ions are held in fixed positions by strong attractions in the solid and cannot move; melting or dissolving frees them, and the mobile ions carry the current.
choices.rationale: Correct: conduction needs mobile charge carriers. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are present in the solid but fixed in the lattice; in the liquid or solution they can move.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ionic bonds exist only in solution, so the solid contains neutral atoms and the ions form only when the compound melts or dissolves.
choices.rationale: The solid is already made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a lattice, so ions do not form only on melting or dissolving.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electrons in solid NaCl are held tightly by chloride ions, and heating or dissolving the solid lets those electrons move freely as the current.
choices.rationale: The current in molten or dissolved NaCl is carried by moving ions, not by free electrons, and the electrons stay on their ions.

title: explain electrical conductivity data for an ionic compound in terms of mobile charged particles in the lattice, liquid a (variant 1)
stem:
A student measures the conductivity of calcium chloride, CaCl₂, in three forms and records the results.
Solid CaCl₂: no current
Molten CaCl₂ at 772°C: large current
CaCl₂ dissolved in water: large current
Which explanation is consistent with all three results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the solid, the Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are locked in lattice positions and cannot move; as a liquid or in solution they can move, and the moving ions carry the charge.
choices.rationale: Correct: conductivity requires mobile charged particles; the ions are fixed in the solid and free to move in the liquid and in solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Melting transforms the CaCl₂ lattice into a metal, and the delocalized electrons of the metal carry the current.
choices.rationale: Molten CaCl₂ is a liquid of Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions and does not become a metal, so there is no sea of electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions exist only after the solid is dissolved or melted, when the solid separates into neutral atoms.
choices.rationale: The solid already consists of Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, and dissolving or melting only frees them to move.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The current in the liquid and solution is carried by electrons that are released as the ionic bonds break.
choices.rationale: The electrons stay with the chloride and calcium ions, and the charge is carried by the ions themselves.

title: explain electrical conductivity data for an ionic compound in terms of mobile charged particles in the lattice, liquid a (variant 2)
stem:
A student measures electrical conductivity of three samples.
Copper metal, solid: large current
Potassium bromide, KBr, solid: no current
Potassium bromide, KBr, molten at 734°C: large current
Which statement about the charge carriers in these samples is consistent with all three results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In solid KBr the electrons are delocalized, as in copper, but they are blocked by the potassium ions until the KBr melts.
choices.rationale: Ionic solids do not have delocalized electrons, and the nonconduction of solid KBr is due to ions being fixed in the lattice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In copper the current is carried by mobile electrons, in molten KBr by mobile ions, and in solid KBr neither electrons nor ions are free to move.
choices.rationale: Correct: copper conducts through delocalized electrons, molten KBr conducts through mobile K⁺ and Br⁻ ions, and solid KBr has ions fixed in a lattice with localized electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In copper and in molten KBr the current is carried by moving ions, but solid KBr contains no ions.
choices.rationale: The metal conducts through delocalized electrons, not ions, and solid KBr does contain K⁺ and Br⁻ ions that are simply fixed in place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In all three samples the current is carried by electrons, but solid KBr has too few electrons to carry a current.
choices.rationale: Molten KBr conducts through ions and not electrons, and the number of electrons in solid KBr is not the reason for its nonconduction.

title: explain electrical conductivity data for an ionic compound in terms of mobile charged particles in the lattice, liquid a (variant 3)
stem:
A student compares two solutions, each prepared by dissolving 0.10 mol of a solid in 1.0 L of water.
Sodium chloride solution: large current
Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, solution: almost no current
Which statement best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sodium chloride solid is held together by hydrogen bonds, which make its solution conduct, whereas sucrose has no hydrogen bonds.
choices.rationale: Sodium chloride is held together by attractions between ions and not by hydrogen bonds, and sucrose actually forms hydrogen bonds with water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sucrose molecules are too large to move through water, but sodium chloride particles are small enough to carry charge.
choices.rationale: The size of the particles does not determine conductivity, and the sucrose molecules do move through water but carry no charge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sodium chloride separates into mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that carry charge, whereas sucrose dissolves as neutral molecules that carry no net charge.
choices.rationale: Correct: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) gives charged carriers; sucrose dissolves without ionizing, so the particles are neutral.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sodium chloride releases free electrons into the water, whereas sucrose keeps all of its electrons.
choices.rationale: Conduction in solution is carried by ions and not by free electrons, which are not released when NaCl dissolves.

title: use atomic radii to identify the type of alloy and explain the change in hardness at the particle level
stem: A pure metal M (atomic radius 150 pm) is soft and very malleable. A small amount of element Z (atomic radius 62 pm) is mixed into molten M, and the cooled alloy is harder and less malleable than pure M. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atoms of Z take the places of atoms of M in the lattice, and because they are slightly different in size they bond covalently with M atoms.
choices.rationale: Substitutional alloys form when the atoms have similar radii, but Z is far smaller than M, so it cannot replace an M atom in the lattice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atoms of Z fit into the spaces between M atoms and interfere with the sliding of layers of M atoms past one another.
choices.rationale: Correct: radii differ by more than about 15 percent (62 vs 150 pm), so Z is small enough to occupy interstitial sites between the M atoms. These interstitial atoms block layers from sliding, which raises hardness and lowers malleability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atoms of Z remove delocalized electrons from M atoms, so the alloy is held together by ionic bonds.
choices.rationale: The alloy remains metallic, with delocalized electrons shared among the atoms, and Z does not remove electrons to form an ionic compound.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atoms of Z are much smaller than M atoms, so they pack the lattice more loosely, letting layers of M slide more easily.
choices.rationale: Small atoms in the interstices fill space between M atoms and make sliding harder, not easier.

title: use atomic radii to identify the type of alloy and explain the change in hardness at the particle level (variant 1)
stem: A pure metal J (atomic radius 128 pm) is soft and malleable. It is melted with a metal L (atomic radius 134 pm) in a 7:3 ratio, and the cooled alloy is harder than pure J while still conducting electricity well. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for these observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atoms of L fit into the empty spaces between J atoms, which blocks layers from sliding and removes the delocalized electrons.
choices.rationale: Interstitial sites are filled by much smaller atoms, and L at 134 pm is slightly larger than J, so it cannot fit into the gaps, and delocalized electrons are not removed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atoms of L and J form ionic bonds, and the ionic lattice is rigid, which explains the hardness.
choices.rationale: Two metals do not transfer electrons to form ions, so the alloy is held together by metallic bonding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atoms of L are nearly the same size as J atoms, so the alloy has exactly the same hardness as pure J.
choices.rationale: Similar size makes a substitutional alloy possible, but the small mismatch distorts the layers and measurably increases hardness, as in brass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atoms of L replace some J atoms in the lattice; their slightly different size distorts the regular layers and makes sliding more difficult, while the delocalized electrons still conduct.
choices.rationale: Correct: radii of 128 and 134 pm differ by about 5 percent, so L replaces J in the lattice (substitutional alloy), and the shared delocalized electrons still conduct.

title: use atomic radii to identify the type of alloy and explain the change in hardness at the particle level (variant 2)
stem: A pure metal T (atomic radius 140 pm) is melted with a small amount of element N (atomic radius 55 pm). The resulting alloy is harder than pure T and shows less malleability. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for these observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atoms of N are small enough to sit in the gaps between T atoms, and these interstitial atoms hinder layers of T atoms from sliding past each other.
choices.rationale: Correct: a radius of 55 pm is much smaller than 140 pm, so N occupies interstitial sites; blocking of layer sliding raises hardness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atoms of N replace atoms of T in the lattice, and their equal charge keeps the layers aligned.
choices.rationale: N is far too small to replace T atoms in a metal lattice, and a substitutional alloy needs similar radii.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atoms of N bond to T atoms through hydrogen bonds, which make the alloy harder.
choices.rationale: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular attractions between molecules and are not the explanation for hardness in a metallic alloy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atoms of N make the T atoms smaller, so the whole lattice contracts and becomes brittle like an ionic solid.
choices.rationale: The T atoms keep their size, and the alloy is held together by metallic bonding, not ionic bonding.

title: use atomic radii to identify the type of alloy and explain the change in hardness at the particle level (variant 3)
stem: A pure metal D (atomic radius 125 pm) is melted with an equal number of atoms of metal E (atomic radius 131 pm). The alloy is harder than pure D and conducts electricity. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for these observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atoms of E occupy the spaces between atoms of D, because E atoms are larger and fill gaps better.
choices.rationale: Interstitial atoms must be much smaller than the host atoms, and E at 131 pm is slightly larger than D, so it cannot fit into the gaps.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atoms of E transfer electrons to atoms of D, so the alloy is a hard ionic solid that conducts only when molten.
choices.rationale: Two metals do not transfer electrons to form an ionic solid, and the alloy conducts as a solid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atoms of E and D form network covalent bonds, which are directional and prevent conduction.
choices.rationale: The alloy conducts electricity, which a network covalent solid with localized electrons would not do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atoms of E substitute for atoms of D in the lattice, and the difference in size disrupts the regular layers so they slide less easily, while delocalized electrons are retained.
choices.rationale: Correct: radii of 125 and 131 pm are within about 5 percent, so E replaces D atoms in the lattice (substitutional alloy); the metallic bonding and conductivity are retained.

title: explain trends in metallic melting temperature using the number of delocalized electrons per atom and the size of the me
stem: Melting temperatures: sodium, Na, 98°C; potassium, K, 63°C; magnesium, Mg, 650°C. Which statement is consistent with all three values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Melting temperature rises with atomic mass, because heavier atoms need more energy to move.
choices.rationale: K is heavier than Na and Mg is lighter than K, yet K melts lower than Na and Mg melts far higher than K, so mass does not predict the trend.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Melting temperature depends on both the number of delocalized electrons each atom contributes and the size of the metal cores; Mg has two electrons per atom and K has the largest cores, so Mg melts highest and K lowest.
choices.rationale: Correct: K (63°C) is heavier and larger than Na (98°C) and melts lower, so larger cores weaken the attraction; Mg (650°C) contributes two delocalized electrons and has a smaller core, so it has the stronger metallic bonding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Melting temperature rises as the metal cores get larger, because larger cores hold more electrons in the sea.
choices.rationale: K has larger cores than Na and melts lower, so larger cores do not give higher melting temperatures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Magnesium melts highest because it forms ionic bonds with itself by giving up two electrons, whereas sodium and potassium form metallic bonds.
choices.rationale: Magnesium metal is held together by metallic bonding, as are sodium and potassium, and a metal does not form ionic bonds with its own atoms.

title: explain trends in metallic melting temperature using the number of delocalized electrons per atom and the size of the me (variant 1)
stem: Melting temperatures: lithium, Li, 181°C; rubidium, Rb, 39°C; barium, Ba, 727°C. Which statement is consistent with all three values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rb melts lowest because its heavier atoms vibrate more slowly, so it needs less energy to melt.
choices.rationale: Slower vibration of heavier atoms is not a factor that sets the strength of metallic bonding, and the trend follows core size and electron count.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ba melts highest because it is a metal with more protons, and the number of protons alone sets the melting temperature.
choices.rationale: Rb has more protons than Li but melts lower, so proton count alone cannot determine melting temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attraction between cores and delocalized electrons is strengthened by more electrons per atom and by smaller cores, so Ba (two electrons) melts highest and Rb (large cores) melts lowest.
choices.rationale: Correct: Li (181) > Rb (39) shows that larger cores lower the melting temperature within a group; Ba (727) shows that two electrons per atom raise it greatly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Li melts higher than Rb because Li atoms are held together by ionic bonds and Rb atoms are not.
choices.rationale: Lithium and rubidium are both metals held by metallic bonding, and neither forms ionic bonds with its own atoms.

title: explain trends in metallic melting temperature using the number of delocalized electrons per atom and the size of the me (variant 2)
stem: Melting temperatures: sodium, Na, 98°C; cesium, Cs, 29°C; calcium, Ca, 842°C. Which statement is consistent with all three values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cs melts lowest because Cs atoms have more electrons, and more electrons in an atom always weaken metallic bonding.
choices.rationale: The number of core electrons in an atom is not the cause, and the effect is due to larger cores having a weaker attraction for the delocalized electrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ca contributes two delocalized electrons per atom, which raises its melting temperature, while the large cores of Cs spread the attraction over a larger volume, giving the lowest melting temperature.
choices.rationale: Correct: Cs is a larger atom than Na with the same one delocalized electron, so it melts lower; Ca gives two electrons per atom and melts much higher.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ca melts highest because heavier atoms have stronger bonds, and Ca is heavier than Na and Cs.
choices.rationale: Cs is heavier than Ca and melts far lower, so atomic mass does not explain the melting temperatures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Na melts higher than Cs because Na atoms have more delocalized electrons than Cs atoms.
choices.rationale: Na and Cs each contribute one delocalized electron per atom, so the difference between them is due to core size and not electron count.

title: explain trends in metallic melting temperature using the number of delocalized electrons per atom and the size of the me (variant 3)
stem: Melting temperatures: potassium, K, 63°C; rubidium, Rb, 39°C; strontium, Sr, 777°C. Which statement is consistent with all three values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sr melts highest because it contributes two delocalized electrons per atom, and Rb melts lower than K because its larger cores attract the electron sea less strongly.
choices.rationale: Correct: Rb has larger cores than K, with the same one electron per atom, so it melts lower; Sr gives two electrons per atom and melts far higher.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sr melts highest because its atoms have larger radii than K and Rb, and larger cores bind more strongly.
choices.rationale: Larger cores weaken the attraction, as Rb melting lower than K shows, so a large radius cannot be the reason Sr melts highest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rb melts lowest because its atoms are heavier, and heavier atoms form weaker covalent bonds.
choices.rationale: Metals are not held together by covalent bonds between atoms, and mass does not set metallic bond strength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: K and Rb melt at low temperatures because they form molecular solids with weak forces between molecules.
choices.rationale: Potassium and rubidium are metals held by metallic bonding and do not exist as molecules, so they have no intermolecular forces.

title: build a Lewis diagram from the valence electron count and count all nonbonding pairs, including the extra pairs on an ex
stem: The ICl₄⁻ ion has iodine as the central atom bonded to four chlorine atoms. How many lone pairs (nonbonding electron pairs, counting those on all atoms) appear in its best Lewis diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 12 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts only the 12 lone pairs on the chlorine atoms and omits the 2 lone pairs left on iodine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 16 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It would need 40 electrons, because it places four lone pairs on iodine, but the ion has only 36 valence electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 28 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts nonbonding electrons, 28, and not pairs, which is the number of electrons and not the number of pairs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 14 lone pairs
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 7 + 4(7) + 1 = 36. Four I–Cl single bonds use 8 electrons; the chlorine atoms take 3 lone pairs each, 24 electrons; the remaining 4 electrons give 2 lone pairs on iodine. Total lone pairs = 12 + 2 = 14.

title: build a Lewis diagram from the valence electron count and count all nonbonding pairs, including the extra pairs on an ex (variant 1)
stem: BrF₃ has bromine as the central atom bonded to three fluorine atoms. How many lone pairs (nonbonding electron pairs, counting those on all atoms) appear in its best Lewis diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 9 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts only the lone pairs on fluorine and forgets the 2 lone pairs on bromine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 11 lone pairs
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 7 + 3(7) = 28. Three Br–F bonds use 6 electrons; fluorine atoms take 18 electrons as 9 lone pairs; the remaining 4 electrons give 2 lone pairs on bromine. Total = 9 + 2 = 11.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 22 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts nonbonding electrons, 22, rather than pairs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 12 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It places 3 lone pairs on bromine, which would require 30 valence electrons and so does not match the 28 available.

title: build a Lewis diagram from the valence electron count and count all nonbonding pairs, including the extra pairs on an ex (variant 2)
stem: SF₄ has sulfur as the central atom bonded to four fluorine atoms. How many lone pairs (nonbonding electron pairs, counting those on all atoms) appear in its best Lewis diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 13 lone pairs
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 6 + 4(7) = 34. Four S–F bonds use 8 electrons; fluorine atoms take 24 electrons as 12 lone pairs; the remaining 2 electrons give 1 lone pair on sulfur. Total = 12 + 1 = 13.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 12 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts the lone pairs on fluorine only and omits the one lone pair on sulfur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 26 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts the 26 nonbonding electrons and not the 13 pairs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 14 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It puts 2 lone pairs on sulfur, which would need 36 valence electrons, but SF₄ has only 34.

title: build a Lewis diagram from the valence electron count and count all nonbonding pairs, including the extra pairs on an ex (variant 3)
stem: The triiodide ion, I₃⁻, has one iodine atom in the center bonded to two terminal iodine atoms. How many lone pairs (nonbonding electron pairs, counting those on all atoms) appear in its best Lewis diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 6 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts only the lone pairs on the terminal iodine atoms and omits the 3 on the central atom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 9 lone pairs
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 3(7) + 1 = 22. Two I–I bonds use 4 electrons; each terminal iodine takes 3 lone pairs, 12 electrons; the remaining 6 electrons give 3 lone pairs on the central iodine. Total = 6 + 3 = 9.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 18 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It counts nonbonding electrons, 18, not pairs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 8 lone pairs
choices.rationale: It gives the central atom only an octet, with 2 lone pairs, and so leaves 2 electrons unplaced.

title: deduce the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms from the formula by combining the valence electron count an
stem: Diazene, N₂H₂, has each nitrogen atom bonded to one hydrogen atom and to the other nitrogen atom. In its best Lewis diagram every nitrogen atom has an octet and each hydrogen atom has two electrons. How many electron pairs are shared between the two nitrogen atoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One pair, a single bond
choices.rationale: A single N–N bond with two lone pairs on each nitrogen requires 14 valence electrons, but only 12 are available.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three pairs, a triple bond
choices.rationale: A triple bond would use 6 electrons for the N–N link and leave 2 electrons that must sit on one nitrogen as a lone pair, giving that atom 10 electrons, which breaks the octet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zero pairs, because the nitrogen atoms are joined only through the hydrogen atoms
choices.rationale: The problem states that each nitrogen is bonded to the other nitrogen, and hydrogen can form only one bond.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two pairs, a double bond
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 2(5) + 2(1) = 12. The two N–H bonds use 4 electrons. If the N–N link were a single bond (2 electrons), two lone pairs on each nitrogen would need 8 more electrons, a total of 14, which exceeds 12. With a double bond (4 electrons) and one lone pair on each nitrogen (4 electrons), the total is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 and every nitrogen has 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 electrons.

title: deduce the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms from the formula by combining the valence electron count an (variant 1)
stem: In the molecule C₂H₂F₂, each carbon atom is bonded to one hydrogen atom, one fluorine atom and the other carbon atom. Every carbon atom has an octet in the best Lewis diagram. How many electron pairs are shared between the two carbon atoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One pair, a single bond
choices.rationale: A single C–C bond would leave each carbon with only six electrons, which is short of an octet, and 2 valence electrons would remain unplaced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three pairs, a triple bond
choices.rationale: A triple bond would require 6 electrons for the carbon link, but only 4 remain after bonds to H and F and the fluorine lone pairs are drawn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two pairs, a double bond
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 2(4) + 2(1) + 2(7) = 24. C–H and C–F bonds use 8 electrons and the fluorine lone pairs use 12, leaving 4 electrons for the C–C link, which is a double bond (check, each carbon has 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 electrons).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four pairs, because each carbon needs four bonds to the other carbon atom
choices.rationale: Four shared pairs would place 8 electrons between the carbons, more than the 4 available.

title: deduce the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms from the formula by combining the valence electron count an (variant 2)
stem: In ethyne, C₂H₂, each carbon atom is bonded to one hydrogen atom and to the other carbon atom. Every carbon atom has an octet in the best Lewis diagram. How many electron pairs are shared between the two carbon atoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One pair, a single bond, with a lone pair on each carbon
choices.rationale: A single bond plus lone pairs would use only 4 + 2 + 4 = 10 electrons, but each carbon would have just 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 electrons, short of an octet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two pairs, a double bond
choices.rationale: A double bond would leave each carbon with 2 + 4 = 6 electrons, and 2 valence electrons would be left over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Three pairs, a triple bond
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 2(4) + 2(1) = 10. The two C–H bonds use 4 electrons, leaving 6 electrons for the C–C link, which is a triple bond; each carbon then has 2 + 6 = 8 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zero pairs, because carbon atoms do not bond to each other
choices.rationale: Carbon atoms readily bond to each other, and the problem states that each carbon is bonded to the other.

title: deduce the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms from the formula by combining the valence electron count an (variant 3)
stem: In hydrazine, N₂H₄, each nitrogen atom is bonded to two hydrogen atoms and to the other nitrogen atom. Every nitrogen atom has an octet in the best Lewis diagram. How many electron pairs are shared between the two nitrogen atoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two pairs, a double bond
choices.rationale: A double bond would need 4 electrons, leaving too few for the lone pairs, and each nitrogen would then exceed eight electrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three pairs, a triple bond
choices.rationale: A triple bond would give each nitrogen 10 electrons or more, which breaks the octet limit for a second-period atom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two pairs, because every nitrogen must have two bonds to another nitrogen to complete an octet
choices.rationale: Each nitrogen reaches an octet using its two N–H bonds, one N–N bond and a lone pair, so no extra N–N bond is needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: One pair, a single bond
choices.rationale: Correct: valence electrons = 2(5) + 4(1) = 14. Four N–H bonds use 8 electrons; the N–N single bond uses 2; the remaining 4 electrons are one lone pair on each nitrogen. Each nitrogen then has 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 electrons.

title: use all resonance contributors to predict the average bond order and the average formal charge on equivalent atoms
stem: The nitrate ion, NO₃⁻, has three equivalent resonance contributors. In each, nitrogen has formal charge +1 and forms one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds; the doubly bonded oxygen has formal charge 0 and the other two oxygen atoms each have formal charge −1. Which statement describes the real ion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each N–O bond has bond order 1.5, and each oxygen atom carries −0.5.
choices.rationale: Bond order 1.5 and −0.5 belong to ions with two contributors such as NO₂⁻, but NO₃⁻ has three contributors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: One N–O bond is a double bond and two are single bonds, and the oxygen atoms carry charges of 0, −1 and −1.
choices.rationale: This describes a single contributor, but the real ion is a hybrid in which the three N–O bonds are identical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each N–O bond has bond order 4/3, and each oxygen atom carries an average charge of −2/3.
choices.rationale: Correct: the bonds per N–O link total 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 spread over 3 equivalent positions, so the bond order is 4/3. The oxygen charges (0, −1, −1) average to −2/3 per oxygen, and nitrogen stays at +1, so the total is +1 − 2 = −1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each N–O bond has bond order 1, and each oxygen atom carries −1.
choices.rationale: Three oxygen atoms at −1 plus nitrogen at +1 would give −2 overall, which does not match the −1 charge of the ion.

title: use all resonance contributors to predict the average bond order and the average formal charge on equivalent atoms (variant 1)
stem: The nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, has two equivalent resonance contributors. In each, nitrogen has formal charge 0, one oxygen forms an N=O double bond with formal charge 0, and the other oxygen forms an N–O single bond with formal charge −1. Which statement describes the real ion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One N–O bond is a double bond and the other is a single bond, and one oxygen carries −1.
choices.rationale: This is one contributor and not the real ion, where both N–O bonds are equal in length and strength.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each N–O bond has bond order 4/3, and each oxygen atom carries −2/3.
choices.rationale: 4/3 and −2/3 are the values for an ion with three equivalent contributors such as NO₃⁻ or CO₃²⁻.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each N–O bond has bond order 2, and each oxygen atom carries −0.5.
choices.rationale: The actual bond order is not 2, because the double bond is shared between both oxygen atoms across the contributors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each N–O bond has bond order 1.5, and each oxygen atom carries an average charge of −0.5.
choices.rationale: Correct: the bond order is (2 + 1) ÷ 2 = 1.5, and the oxygen charge averages (0 − 1) ÷ 2 = −0.5; nitrogen remains 0, so the total is −1.

title: use all resonance contributors to predict the average bond order and the average formal charge on equivalent atoms (variant 2)
stem: The carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, has three equivalent resonance contributors. In each, carbon has formal charge 0 and forms one C=O double bond and two C–O single bonds; the doubly bonded oxygen has formal charge 0 and the other two oxygen atoms have formal charge −1. Which statement describes the real ion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each C–O bond has bond order 1.5, and each oxygen atom carries −0.5.
choices.rationale: Bond order 1.5 and −0.5 describe two contributors, but carbonate has three, so the shared double bond is spread over three positions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each C–O bond has bond order 1, and each oxygen atom carries −1.
choices.rationale: This ignores the double bond altogether, and three oxygen atoms at −1 would give −3 overall, not the −2 charge of the ion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: One C–O bond is a double bond and two are single bonds, and the oxygen atoms carry 0, −1 and −1.
choices.rationale: This describes a single contributor and treats one of the three equivalent oxygen atoms as different from the others.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each C–O bond has bond order 4/3, and each oxygen atom carries an average charge of −2/3.
choices.rationale: Correct: the bond order is (2 + 1 + 1) ÷ 3 = 4/3, and the oxygen charge averages (0 − 1 − 1) ÷ 3 = −2/3; with carbon at 0, the total is −2.

title: use all resonance contributors to predict the average bond order and the average formal charge on equivalent atoms (variant 3)
stem: The acetate ion, CH₃COO⁻, has two equivalent resonance contributors. In each, carbon forms either a C=O double bond or a C–O single bond with each oxygen. A single C–O bond is about 143 pm long and a C=O double bond is about 120 pm long. Which statement describes the two C–O bonds in the real ion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One C–O bond is about 143 pm and the other is about 120 pm, and the ion switches rapidly between them.
choices.rationale: Resonance contributors are not structures that interconvert; the ion is a single hybrid, in which both C–O bonds are identical.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two C–O bonds are equal in length, with a value between 120 pm and 143 pm, because the real ion is a hybrid of both contributors.
choices.rationale: Correct: the bond order of each C–O bond is (2 + 1) ÷ 2 = 1.5, so the length falls between the single-bond and double-bond values and both are equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both C–O bonds are about 143 pm, because the negative charge makes both bonds single.
choices.rationale: The negative charge is shared between the oxygen atoms and does not turn both bonds into single bonds, which would make a bond order of 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both C–O bonds are about 120 pm, because the double bond is always present on both oxygen atoms.
choices.rationale: A bond order of 2 for both bonds would require two double bonds to carbon, which exceeds the bonding of one carbon in this ion.

title: distinguish formal charge from oxidation number for the same atom in the same species
stem: In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, nitrogen forms four single bonds to hydrogen and has no lone pairs. A student states that formal charge and oxidation number are the same quantity. Which choice gives the formal charge and the oxidation number of nitrogen in NH₄⁺?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formal charge +1, oxidation number +1
choices.rationale: It uses the charge of the ion for both quantities, but oxidation numbers assign shared electrons to the more electronegative atom, which is nitrogen, so nitrogen is negative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formal charge −3, oxidation number −3
choices.rationale: It applies the oxidation number to the formal charge, but formal charge splits each shared pair equally, and a nitrogen with four bonds has +1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formal charge +1, oxidation number −3
choices.rationale: Correct: formal charge = 5 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding electrons − 4 bonds = +1. Oxidation number: hydrogen is +1 (4 × +1 = +4), so N + 4 = +1 gives N = −3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formal charge 0, oxidation number −3
choices.rationale: It miscounts the formal charge as zero, which would need three bonds and a lone pair, as in NH₃, not four bonds.

title: distinguish formal charge from oxidation number for the same atom in the same species (variant 1)
stem: In the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺, oxygen forms three single bonds to hydrogen and has one lone pair. Which choice gives the formal charge and the oxidation number of oxygen in H₃O⁺?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formal charge +1, oxidation number −2
choices.rationale: Correct: formal charge = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. Oxidation number: 3(+1) + O = +1, so O = −2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formal charge −2, oxidation number +1
choices.rationale: This swaps the two values, and the formal charge of oxygen with three bonds and a lone pair is +1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formal charge +1, oxidation number +1
choices.rationale: It uses the ion charge for the oxidation number, but the oxidation number of oxygen bonded to hydrogen is −2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formal charge −2, oxidation number −2
choices.rationale: It assigns oxygen its usual oxidation number as its formal charge, but formal charge splits the shared electrons equally.

title: distinguish formal charge from oxidation number for the same atom in the same species (variant 2)
stem: In the tetrafluoroborate ion, BF₄⁻, boron forms four single bonds to fluorine and has no lone pairs. Which choice gives the formal charge and the oxidation number of boron in BF₄⁻?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formal charge −1, oxidation number +3
choices.rationale: Correct: formal charge = 3 − 0 − 4 = −1. Oxidation number: 4(−1) + B = −1, so B = +3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formal charge +3, oxidation number +3
choices.rationale: It treats the two numbers as the same, but formal charge splits the shared pairs equally, so boron has −1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formal charge −1, oxidation number −1
choices.rationale: It takes the ion charge as both quantities, but fluorine is more electronegative and takes the shared electrons, giving boron +3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formal charge +3, oxidation number −1
choices.rationale: It reverses the two values, though boron has three valence electrons and four bonds, which gives −1 as formal charge.

title: distinguish formal charge from oxidation number for the same atom in the same species (variant 3)
stem: In one Lewis diagram of the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻, sulfur forms three single bonds to oxygen and has one lone pair. Which choice gives the formal charge and the oxidation number of sulfur in this diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formal charge +1, oxidation number +4
choices.rationale: Correct: formal charge = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. Oxidation number: 3(−2) + S = −2, so S = +4.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formal charge +4, oxidation number +4
choices.rationale: It uses the oxidation number for the formal charge, but formal charge assigns bonding electrons equally and gives sulfur +1 here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formal charge +1, oxidation number +1
choices.rationale: It assigns formal charge as the oxidation number, but oxidation numbers give the shared electrons to oxygen, which is more electronegative, so sulfur is +4.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formal charge −2, oxidation number +4
choices.rationale: It takes the ion charge as the formal charge on sulfur, but the charge of the ion is the sum over all four atoms.

title: count sigma and pi bonds and assign hybridization for several atoms in a molecule from its bonding pattern
stem: Acrylonitrile, H₂C=CH–C≡N, is used to make plastics. Its atoms are bonded as shown: a C=C double bond, a C–C single bond and a C≡N triple bond, with two hydrogen atoms on the first carbon and one on the second. Which statement about its bonding is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has 5 sigma bonds and 4 pi bonds, and the carbon in the C≡N group is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: It counts the triple bond as three pi bonds, but every multiple bond contains exactly one sigma bond, so the count of sigma bonds is 6.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds, and the carbon in the C≡N group is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: Correct: sigma bonds are 3 C–H, 1 C=C, 1 C–C and 1 C≡N, a total of 6; pi bonds are 1 in C=C and 2 in C≡N, a total of 3. The nitrile carbon has 2 electron domains (one single bond and one triple bond), so it is sp; the CH₂ carbon has 3 domains and is sp².

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds, and the carbon in the C≡N group is sp² hybridized.
choices.rationale: The carbon in the nitrile group has two electron domains, not three, so it is sp hybridized and not sp².

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds, and the CH₂ carbon is sp³ hybridized.
choices.rationale: The CH₂ carbon has three electron domains, two C–H bonds and one double bond to carbon, so it is sp² and not sp³.

title: count sigma and pi bonds and assign hybridization for several atoms in a molecule from its bonding pattern (variant 1)
stem: Propyne, H₃C–C≡C–H, has a methyl carbon bonded to three hydrogen atoms and a C≡C triple bond to a carbon that is bonded to the last hydrogen. Which statement about its bonding is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and the methyl carbon is sp³ hybridized while both other carbons are sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: Correct: sigma bonds are 3 C–H (methyl), 1 C–C, 1 C≡C and 1 C–H (terminal), a total of 6; pi bonds are 2 in the triple bond. The methyl carbon has 4 domains (sp³), and the two triple-bonded carbons have 2 domains each (sp).

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and the methyl carbon is sp² hybridized.
choices.rationale: The methyl carbon has four single bonds, so it has four electron domains and is sp³, not sp².

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has 5 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds, and the terminal carbon is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: It counts 5 sigma bonds, which treats part of the triple bond as pi bonds only, but a triple bond has 1 sigma bond and 2 pi bonds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and all three carbon atoms are sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: The methyl carbon has four sigma bonds and no pi bonds, so it requires four hybrid orbitals and is sp³.

title: count sigma and pi bonds and assign hybridization for several atoms in a molecule from its bonding pattern (variant 2)
stem: Acetaldehyde, H₃C–CH=O, has a methyl carbon bonded to a second carbon, which is bonded to one hydrogen atom and double bonded to oxygen. Which statement about its bonding is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has 5 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and the carbonyl carbon is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: It counts 5 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, treating the C=O as two pi bonds, and it assigns sp to a carbon with 3 domains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond, and the carbonyl carbon is sp³ hybridized.
choices.rationale: The sigma and pi counts are correct, but the carbonyl carbon has three electron domains, and sp³ would need four.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has 6 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond, and the carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridized.
choices.rationale: Correct: sigma bonds are 3 C–H (methyl), 1 C–C, 1 C–H and 1 C=O, a total of 6; the C=O double bond has 1 pi bond. The carbonyl carbon has 3 electron domains (C, H, O), so it is sp².

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has 7 sigma bonds and 0 pi bonds, because a double bond counts as two sigma bonds.
choices.rationale: A double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi bond, and not two sigma bonds, so the molecule has 6 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond.

title: count sigma and pi bonds and assign hybridization for several atoms in a molecule from its bonding pattern (variant 3)
stem: Acetonitrile, H₃C–C≡N, has a methyl carbon bonded to a carbon that has a triple bond to nitrogen. Which statement about its bonding is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has 5 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and the nitrogen atom is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: Correct: sigma bonds are 3 C–H, 1 C–C and 1 C≡N, a total of 5; pi bonds are 2. Nitrogen has 2 electron domains (one triple bond and one lone pair), so it is sp hybridized.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has 5 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and the methyl carbon is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: The methyl carbon has four sigma bonds and no pi bonds, so it is sp³ and not sp.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has 4 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds, and the nitrogen atom is sp hybridized.
choices.rationale: It counts only 4 sigma bonds and 3 pi bonds, which wrongly treats the triple bond as three pi bonds with no sigma bond.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has 5 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds, and the nitrogen atom is sp³ hybridized.
choices.rationale: Nitrogen has two electron domains, a bond domain and a lone pair, which needs 2 hybrid orbitals and so is sp and not sp³.

title: use electron-domain repulsion, including the greater repulsion of lone pairs, to explain observed deviations in bond ang
stem: The H–X–H bond angles are about 109.5° in CH₄, 107° in NH₃ and 104.5° in H₂O. In each molecule the central atom has four electron domains. Which explanation best accounts for the decrease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nitrogen and oxygen are more electronegative than carbon, so they pull the hydrogen atoms closer together.
choices.rationale: Electronegativity changes bond polarity but does not account for the angle trend through the order of repulsions between domains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lone pairs are attracted to the hydrogen nuclei and pull the hydrogen atoms toward each other.
choices.rationale: Lone pairs do not attract the hydrogen nuclei, and the angle decreases because the lone pair repels the bonding pairs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lone pair repels neighboring electron domains more strongly than a bonding pair does, so as lone pairs replace bonding pairs the bonding pairs are pushed closer together.
choices.rationale: Correct: all three have tetrahedral electron-domain geometry (ideal 109.5°); NH₃ has 1 lone pair and H₂O has 2, and the lone pair-bonding pair repulsion exceeds the bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion, compressing the angle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The central atoms get smaller from carbon to oxygen, so the hydrogen atoms crowd together and the angle must narrow.
choices.rationale: The H–X–H angle in VSEPR is set by repulsions among electron domains and not by the size of the central atom.

title: use electron-domain repulsion, including the greater repulsion of lone pairs, to explain observed deviations in bond ang (variant 1)
stem: In SF₆ every F–S–F angle between adjacent fluorine atoms is 90°. In BrF₅, which also has six electron domains around the central atom, the angle between the axial fluorine and each basal fluorine is about 85°. Which explanation best accounts for the smaller angle in BrF₅?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bromine is larger than sulfur, so the fluorine atoms are forced closer together.
choices.rationale: The angle change is explained by repulsion of electron domains and not by the size of the central atom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorine is more electronegative in BrF₅ than in SF₆, so the F atoms pull toward each other.
choices.rationale: The fluorine atoms are the same element in both species and the bond polarity does not set the angle in VSEPR.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lone pair on bromine attracts the fluorine atoms, which pulls them toward the lone pair and increases the angle.
choices.rationale: Lone pairs repel, not attract, the bonding pairs, and the observed angle gets smaller, not larger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lone pair on bromine repels the bonding pairs more strongly than they repel one another, pushing the fluorine atoms away from the lone pair and closer to the axial fluorine.
choices.rationale: Correct: both have octahedral electron-domain geometry; BrF₅ has one lone pair, which repels bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other and bends the F atoms away from it.

title: use electron-domain repulsion, including the greater repulsion of lone pairs, to explain observed deviations in bond ang (variant 2)
stem: In the trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry, the ideal angle between two equatorial positions is 120°. In SF₄, which has this electron-domain geometry, the equatorial F–S–F angle is about 102°. Which explanation best accounts for the smaller angle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sulfur has 34 valence electrons, which compresses every bond angle by the same amount.
choices.rationale: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons and the molecule has 34 in total, and the number of electrons does not equally compress the angles of the molecule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lone pair attracts the equatorial fluorine atoms and pulls them toward each other.
choices.rationale: A lone pair repels bonding pairs, so it pushes the fluorine atoms away from it and does not pull them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fluorine atoms are small, so they can approach each other more closely than the bonding pairs would allow.
choices.rationale: Bond angles in VSEPR come from repulsions between electron domains and not from the sizes of the outer atoms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lone pair sits in an equatorial position and repels the two equatorial bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other, pushing them closer together.
choices.rationale: Correct: SF₄ has 5 electron domains (4 bonds, 1 lone pair); the lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly than they repel one another, so the equatorial angle falls below 120°.

title: use electron-domain repulsion, including the greater repulsion of lone pairs, to explain observed deviations in bond ang (variant 3)
stem: The O–S–O bond angle is about 109.5° in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, and about 106° in the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻, in Lewis diagrams that give sulfur an octet in both ions. Which explanation best accounts for the smaller angle in SO₃²⁻?

choices.label: A
choices.text: SO₃²⁻ has fewer oxygen atoms, so there is less space for them and they must be closer together.
choices.rationale: Having fewer oxygen atoms would leave more room around sulfur and not less, and the angle changes because of the lone pair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sulfur in SO₃²⁻ has a lone pair that repels the three bonding pairs more strongly than they repel one another, compressing the O–S–O angle.
choices.rationale: Correct: SO₄²⁻ has 4 bonding domains and no lone pair (tetrahedral, 109.5°); SO₃²⁻ has 3 bonding domains and 1 lone pair (trigonal pyramidal), and the lone pair compresses the angles below 109.5°.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The extra negative charge of SO₃²⁻ attracts the oxygen atoms to each other.
choices.rationale: Negative charge does not attract oxygen atoms to each other, and they carry partial negative charges that repel each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sulfite sulfur is bonded to oxygen by double bonds, which are shorter and so pull the oxygen atoms together.
choices.rationale: In the octet-rule diagram of SO₃²⁻ all S–O bonds are single, and bond length is not what sets the angle.
